The possible payer is the hotel owner or manager controlling the operating budget, not necessarily the receptionist. Neither recurring workload nor willingness to pay €25/month is established. The precise Riga signal is an official notice announcing a temporary route 95 service from 4 November: it supports the existence of dated transport changes, but not relevance to hotel arrival routes or customer demand. evidence.title: Air travel made up 17.2% of trips in 2025
evidence.excerpt: In 2025, EU residents made 1.2 billion trips, of which 81.4% were made by land, 17.2% by air and 1.4% by waterways. uncertainty: Receptionists at small Riga hotels serving relevant transport routes repeatedly spend time checking and explaining arrival journeys.
Hotel owners or managers would consider €25/month if verified cards save enough staff time without increasing error risk or checking work.
Propose a permission-based, non-guest-facing discovery step with two receptionists: establish recurring question categories and handling time without collecting guest personal data.

Frequency, handling time and seasonality of transport questions at the proposed hotels.
dissent: A maintained route sheet or existing reply template could provide the same benefit with less daily review work.
A narrow segment sharing frequently changing routes might still merit discovery, but neither EU travel totals nor this single Riga notice identifies that segment.
Scheduling documentation and supplier prices concern capability and input costs, not buyer value or demand.

say: Do not set the gate on all transport questions: count only questions where a fresh notice could change the answer relative to a maintained route sheet. The supplied temporary-route notice establishes that changes occur, not how often they affect hotel arrivals. My proposed screening threshold—not an established benchmark—is at least 3 such questions per hotel per day, each taking at least 2 minutes with the maintained sheet, spread across at least 5 days in a 14-day observation window. uncertainty: Per-hotel frequency and handling time of arrival questions whose answers actually depend on fresh notices, rather than stable route information.
Incremental card savings after reading/checking overhead, the hotel's value for saved time, and willingness to pay the hypothetical €25 monthly price.
dissent: Even frequent, slow questions may reflect a poorly designed route sheet rather than a need for daily cards. A clearer maintained sheet with change-triggered updates could capture the same benefit with less attention overhead; daily cards must outperform that comparator, not merely usual replies.
